ta-l1d19q3-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph introducing the treatment of magnitude in two articles: whether magnitude belongs to God and what it is, and the sign of the persons' equality in magnitude, namely their being in one another.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3510.summary: First argument that magnitude does not belong to God. Magnitude is a condition of matter, and no material condition is said of God except metaphorically.
claims: Magnitude is a material condition.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3513.summary: Second argument. Great and small are opposed, but every small thing is also great, as every few is many (Metaphysics 10), so every great thing seems also small. God is not small, so he is not great.
claims: Great and small are relative.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3516.summary: Third argument. Magnitude is continuous quantity, and there can be no continuity in God, who is simple and indivisible.
claims: Magnitude is continuous quantity.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3520.summary: Anticipates the reply that God is great by a quantity of power. But by his power God is called powerful, and here power is distinguished from magnitude, so magnitude of power is not meant.
claims: Power and magnitude are listed separately.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3523.summary: Sed contra from Psalm 146:5: great is our God and great is his power.
claims: Scripture calls God great.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3529.summary: Thomas's determination. In God there can be only quantity of power (virtus), and since equality follows some species of quantity, it is only by power. According to the Philosopher, virtus is the ultimate of a thing's potency, a perfection, and each thing is perfect when it reaches its proper virtus. So virtus can be considered in every way in which something reaches its ultimate, which happens in three ways: in operations, in which there are degrees of perfection (virtue makes its possessor good and its work good, Ethics 2); with respect to a thing's being, as something has the power always to be; and in the fullness of perfection of the being itself, as it reaches the ultimate of its nature, as the virtus of a circle is said to be when it fully attains its definition. So divine virtus considered as perfection for operation is operative power; as perfection of divine being itself it is eternity; and as the completeness of the perfection of the divine nature it is magnitude. This is clear from Lombard's proof of equal magnitude from the whole fullness of the Father's nature being in the Son, and from Augustine's saying that in things not great in bulk, to be greater is to be better, as we call a person great who is perfect in knowledge and virtue. As by the power of his omnipotence God founds all operative powers and works in them, so by the power of his eternity he establishes and confirms all duration, and by the power of his magnitude he fills and contains all things.
claims: God's only quantity is quantity of virtus, which is threefold: operative power, eternity, and magnitude.
Divine magnitude is the completeness of the perfection of the divine nature.
By magnitude God fills and contains all things.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3532.summary: Reply to the first argument. Magnitude by the concept of its genus, quantity, is a condition of matter and is not predicated of God in that way, but by the concept of its differentia, which consists in completeness, as we say someone grows from small to great when they reach complete quantity.
claims: Magnitude is said of God by its differentia, completeness, not its genus.
concepts: genus and differentia in divine names

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3535.summary: Reply to the second argument. Continuous quantity is divided infinitely but not increased infinitely, so by infinite division any small thing can have something smaller relative to which it seems great, but not every great thing has something greater relative to which it is small, as with the heavens' quantity. Moreover, if great and small are taken not relatively but absolutely, as quantity determined to a species, then although every lesser is greater than something, not every lesser is small, nor every greater great. Still, Dionysius says God is called small as well as great, taking 'small' for subtle, as he penetrates everything, even the deepest thoughts, and as principles are said to be small in quantity and great in power.
claims: Great and small taken absolutely are not convertible.
God is called 'small' in the sense of subtle, penetrating all things.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3538.summary: Reply to the third argument. Continuity follows dimensive magnitude, not magnitude of power, which alone is to be understood in God.
claims: Only magnitude of power, not dimensive magnitude, is in God.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3542.summary: Reply to the fourth argument, from the body: virtus is said not only with respect to operation, where it is called power, but in the other ways explained.
claims: Virtus covers power, eternity, and magnitude.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3554.summary: First argument that the Father is not in the Son nor conversely. The Philosopher lists eight ways of being in, none of which fits the Father's being in the Son or conversely: as whole in parts or conversely, as genus in species or conversely, as in place, as form in matter, as in a mover (a kingdom in its king), or as in an end.
claims: None of Aristotle's eight modes of 'being in' fits the persons.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3557.summary: Second argument. When one thing is with another as distinct from it, one is not in the other. The Son is 'with' the Father ('the Word was with God', John 1:1).
claims: Being 'with' excludes being 'in'.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3563.summary: Third argument. In God there is only relation of origin, and the preposition 'in' implies some relation, so in God it can only imply relation of origin. Son and Father do not have the same relation to each other, so either not each is in the other, or not in the same way.
claims: 'In' in God can signify only relation of origin.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3567.summary: Sed contra. Wherever the Father's essence is, the Father is, and the Father's whole essence is in the Son and conversely.
claims: Wherever the Father's essence is, he is.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3570.summary: Second sed contra. In one relative the other is understood, and Father and Son are relatives.
claims: In one relative the other is understood.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3573.summary: Thomas's determination. In the divine persons there are the one same essence and the relations distinguishing them, and by both the Father is said to be in the Son and conversely, according to different authorities. For Augustine, Hilary, and Ambrose, cited by Lombard, it is because of the unity of essence: the Father's essence is in the Son, and the Father does not leave his nature, so where his nature is, there he is (Hilary, Dist. 5). For Damascene it is by the concept of relation, since in one relative the other is understood.
claims: The Father is in the Son both by unity of essence (Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose) and by relation (Damascene).

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3576.summary: Reply to the first argument. Strictly, not all ways of being in are contained in those eight, except by a reduction by likeness, as being in time reduces to being in place, both being as measured in a measure. This mode too can be reduced by likeness. Taken as unity of essence, the Father is in the Son because his essence is in the Son, which reduces to the way a common nature is in a supposit, and so to the way a genus is in a species, though in God there is no genus and species (Dist. 25). Taken as relation, it reduces to the way something is in another as in a moving and efficient principle: though the Father is not the Son's efficient principle, he is his originator, so the Son is in the Father as originated in originator and the Father in the Son as originator in originated. In God the Son is even more properly in the Father by relation than in human things, since by his very relation the Son is a subsistent person, his relation being his personality, which does not happen in other things.
claims: Circumincession reduces to common nature in supposit (by essence) or originated in originator (by relation).
The Son is more properly in the Father than a human son, since his relation is his personality.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3579.summary: Reply to the second argument. One person is said to be 'with' another by reason of distinction, but 'in' another either by essence or by the understanding of relations, since one is understood in the other, though one relative is distinct from the other.
claims: 'With' signifies distinction; 'in' signifies essence or co-understanding of relatives.

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3582.summary: Reply to the third argument. If the Father is in the Son by unity of essence, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father in the same way, and 'in' implies not a real relation but only a conceptual relation, like that between essence and person by which the essence is said to be in the person. If it is by relation, the mode differs according to the Father's and Son's different relations to each other.
claims: By essence, mutual indwelling is the same both ways; by relation, it differs.
concepts: mutual indwelling by essence vs. by relation

ta-l1d19q3-d1e3591.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Your years are from generation to generation' signifies eternity not by multiplicity, since it is one and simple, but as able to contain by its power a great multitude of a lower, divisible measure, as we say there was time before the world not really but in imagination, imagining that additions could have been made to time on the earlier side, all contained under eternity. (2) The whole divine nature is perfectly in each hypostasis, whole and perfect. (3) No human comparison offers an adequate example for divine things: in every likeness there is a greater unlikeness. (4) 'What is not intelligible to a human is possible to God': since the infinite divine nature and power exceed our intellect, nothing we can understand is beyond God's power, but he can do many things we cannot understand, and these can be and are in him; nothing can be in him that is not, nor is there anything in him that could not be, otherwise he would be mutable. (5) Divine truth, from which Scripture comes to us, suffices as the reason or middle term for belief, even if reasons drawn from natures seem to dissent. (6) The Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father because the full divinity is in each: if one lacked what the other had, neither would be perfect, since the giver would give part of his substance and both would have a limit of deity. So the receiver must receive all, and where the Father's whole nature is, he is. (7) Hilary's phrases exclude that the Son's birth is the same (nothing is born of itself) or that he is another thing (what is born of a living being receives at least the same nature in species, and since the divine nature cannot be numerically multiplied, the Son receives numerically the same nature, so he is 'another' person, not 'another thing'). The Son is not by a union of different kinds, like a mule, nor by grafting, but by a likeness united in one numerical nature, which is unity rather than mere likeness. He is living nature from living nature, and his birth does not degenerate from God's nature, as happens when indisposed matter fails to receive the agent's complete form.
claims: Eternity's 'years' signify its capacity to contain divisible time.
In every likeness between God and creatures there is a greater unlikeness.
Divine truth suffices as the ground of belief even against natural reasons.
Full divinity in each person entails their mutual indwelling and numerical unity of nature.

ta-l1d19q3-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 3 introduces divine magnitude and the persons' mutual indwelling as its sign of equality.

ta-l1d19q3-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks whether magnitude belongs to God and what it is. Thomas holds that God's only quantity is quantity of virtus, a thing's ultimate perfection, which is threefold: as perfection for operation it is power, as perfection of being it is eternity, and as completeness of the divine nature's perfection it is magnitude. Magnitude is said of God by its differentia, completeness, not by its material genus, and only as magnitude of power, without continuity. By it God fills and contains all things, and he may also be called 'small' in the sense of subtle.
claims: Divine magnitude is the completeness of the divine nature's perfection, one of three senses of divine virtus alongside power and eternity.

ta-l1d19q3-Dd1e3546.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Father is in the Son and conversely. Thomas holds that they are, by unity of essence (Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose), since where the Father's nature is, he is, and by relation (Damascene), since one relative is understood in the other. These modes reduce to common nature in supposit and to originated in originator. The Son is more properly in the Father than a human son is, since his relation is his personality. 'With' signifies distinction and 'in' signifies essence or co-understanding.
claims: The Father and Son are in each other by unity of essence and by relation.

ta-l1d19q3-Dd1e3586.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 19 interprets eternity's 'years' and the full presence of the divine nature in each hypostasis. It stresses the greater unlikeness in every likeness and the sufficiency of divine truth for belief, and it explains, with Hilary, that full divinity in each person entails their mutual indwelling and numerically one nature.
claims: Full divinity in each person entails mutual indwelling and numerical unity of nature.

ta-l1d19q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 19 treats divine magnitude and its sign, the persons' mutual indwelling. Article 1 holds that God's only quantity is quantity of virtus, a thing's ultimate perfection, which in God is threefold: operative power, eternity as the perfection of being, and magnitude as the completeness of the divine nature's perfection, by which he fills and contains all things. Article 2 holds that the Father and Son are in each other both by unity of essence and by the co-understanding of relatives, reducible to the modes of common nature in supposit and of originated in originator. The Expositio draws from the full divinity in each person their mutual indwelling and numerical unity of nature.
claims: Divine magnitude is the completeness of the divine nature's perfection.
God's virtus is threefold: power, eternity, and magnitude.
The persons are in one another by unity of essence and by relation.
